item.title: One step closer to quantum computers that can correct their own mistakes
item.description: Researchers from Rutgers, IBM and collaborating institutions have shown that a quantum computer can check what is happening inside it and respond while it is running, repeatedly resetting parts of the system to bring chaotic behavior under control. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Universities are making different choices about AI. How will they fit with their public missions?
item.description: Artificial intelligence has moved quickly from an emerging technology to one that is forcing universities to make consequential choices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ALMA catches a dying star mid-transformation, with a ring from its last outburst
item.description: Astronomers have used radio observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to catch a dying star in the middle of a dramatic transformation, and the data show a ring that records its final outburst. The new research was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 18. The paper has been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Identity develops well into adulthood and is linked to better mental well-being
item.description: Identity development is not limited to adolescence, a recent study from the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, shows. Researchers found that identity developed positively from age 27 to 61. A more positively developed identity was associated with higher levels of mental well-being. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supply chain experts say uncertainty will disrupt 4th Quarter
item.description: The results of the Lehigh Business Supply Chain Risk Management Index for the fourth quarter of 2026 show a slight decrease from last quarter's sharp jump in overall risk. Transportation disruption risk remained the highest-rated category, down from its record high in the third quarter but still well above its three-year average. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Molecular sunscreen' may explain why DNA uses thymine despite its vulnerability to UV damage
item.description: Scientists have long sought to understand the complex origins of intelligent life. It remains unclear how biological systems not only formed but survived and persisted under the extreme conditions of primordial Earth's hostile climate. Now, researchers at Texas A&M University are using light-based technologies to uncover new clues to help solve this evolutionary puzzle. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Preliminary Lunar Science Report for Artemis II is out
item.description: On April 1, 2026, the crew of the Artemis II mission launched into space atop NASA's Space Launch System (SLS). Roughly 3 1/2 hours after launch, the rocket's upper stage separated from the Orion spacecraft (Integrity), and astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen began their nearly 10-day journey around the moon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some house cats carry a gut parasite that can infect humans, study finds
item.description: Giardia duodenalis is a microscopic, flagellated parasite that often calls the human and animal gut its home. In most cases, it coexists harmlessly with its host, and most infected pets and people show no signs of illness. However, when it becomes pathogenic, it can cause diarrhea, digestive issues or weight loss. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Atypical B cells shift immune roles as they develop, malaria study finds
item.description: B cells are an important part of the immune system and help the body recognize and fight infections. A group of B cells known as atypical B cells has attracted considerable interest among researchers in recent years. They occur in several infections, but also in connection with vaccinations and certain inflammatory diseases. Despite extensive research, it has long remained unclear how these cells arise and what function they serve. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The gooier marine snow is, the better it is at transporting carbon, new study finds
item.description: In the deep sea, it never stops snowing. The type of snow that falls in the ocean, known as marine snow, is very different from the flaky geometric wonders that fall on land. Marine snow describes tiny clumps of organic and inorganic detritus—think mucus, poop, silt, dead plankton, etc.—that rain from the shallows into the deep. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As the school year settles in, making room for the arts can support everyday well‑being
item.description: As the days darken, making more room for arts-based practices and experiences is one way to bring useful, interesting or sustaining activities into the seasons ahead. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ball or strike? Why the count may change what a baseball umpire sees
item.description: In baseball, a borderline pitch is more likely to be called a strike when the batter has three balls and no strikes than when the count is no balls and two strikes. The official strike zone hasn't changed. The umpire's judgment has. Fuente: Phys.org.

How did a young farmhand change American Christianity forever? After claiming a series of spiritual visions, Joseph Smith was said to have translated... Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: AI platform and database map protein phase separation across species
item.description: Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have developed an AI-powered database and a platform that could enable researchers to more accurately predict which proteins undergo phase separation—a process through which proteins in cells separate like oil droplets in water. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why a tiny number of venture capitalists capture almost all the profit
item.description: Beyond a handful of big names, most venture capitalists are relatively unknown. Who are they, and what distinguishes the superstars from the rest? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Climate fingerprints reveal stronger evidence of human-caused warming after more than 30 years
item.description: The scientific evidence for human-caused global warming is stronger than ever, according to a major new review—despite a U.S. government report questioning the science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Welcome home, Sophie Adenot
item.description: Video: 00:02:54 After 237 days and over 3,700 orbits around Earth aboard the International Space Station, Sophie Adenot is back on Earth! Following a handover to Crew-13, Sophie and her Crew-12 crewmates undocked on 7 October and splashed down off the coast of California the next day. Now back in Europe, Sophie will begin her post-flight data collection and rehabilitation while readjusting to life on Earth after the longest mission in space by a European astronaut so far. Welcome home, Sophie! Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: DNA reveals genetic divide in Australian brolgas, with southern birds facing greater diversity risks
item.description: New research on the brolga, an iconic Australian crane species, has shown important genetic differences between northern and southeastern populations, with evidence that those in western Victoria are at increased risk, likely heightened by the loss of wetlands. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why some anglers always follow the rules
item.description: New research sheds light on why a surprising number of fishers always follow fishing rules, even when enforcement is unlikely and breaking the rules offers a financial reward. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New sensor uses slowed light to detect gravitational pull of tiny objects
item.description: Gravity, the attraction between objects with mass, is the weakest of the four fundamental forces governing physical processes. Detecting the tiny gravitational pull of objects that are just a few millimeters in size and have a very small mass is extremely challenging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI system could transform rabies testing around the world
item.description: Rabies virus detection in cell cultures could soon become faster and more accessible, thanks to the world's first AI system for this purpose, developed by researchers at the University of Surrey's Institute for People-Centered AI (PAI) in collaboration with the Rabies and Viral Zoonoses team at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study explores why Indigenous communities may accept oil extraction despite its harms
item.description: The uneven distribution of oil extraction's impacts and benefits helps explain why some Indigenous communities accept it, newly published research shows. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dos estadounidenses ganan el Nobel de Economía por su innovador modelo que ayuda a gobiernos y bancos centrales de todo el mundo a estabilizar la economía
item.description: La Academia Sueca destacó los aportes de ambos investigadores a los fundamentos microeconómicos de la estabilización macroeconómica. Fuente: BBC News Mundo.

item.title: Model links course design, psychological safety and guided AI use
item.description: University of Phoenix researchers have published a new peer-reviewed study examining how stress, self-regulation, resilience, belonging, psychological safety and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) interact in the experiences of nontraditional online students. The article, "Designing for Persistence in Online Higher Education: A Trauma-Informed, GenAI-Integrated Model for Non-Traditional Learners," was published in Innovative Higher Education. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI platforms offer promise in limiting the illegal wildlife trade
item.description: New University of Kent research has found promising signs that AI platforms have the potential to limit the illegal wildlife trade. The research paper titled "Assessing safeguards against the illegal wildlife trade on AI platforms" is published in Conservation Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computers could finally get to grips with light and matter
item.description: Many of nature's most important processes depend on how particles of matter interact with light and other force-carrying particles. So far, however, it has proven difficult for conventional computers to determine how individual particles behave in these interactions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem
item.description: Popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs, such as Ozempic and Wegovy, have been linked to unexpectedly high rates of nail detachment, hair loss, and scalp inflammation, with some problems occurring several times more frequently among users. Researchers found that weight loss alone could not fully explain the differences, suggesting there may be more to these overlooked symptoms. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
item.description: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: World leaders urged to 'course correct' as UN nature goals fall short
item.description: Nations are steeling for a disappointing report card at this month's U.N. biodiversity summit, with governments falling short on their commitments to protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El Niño sets temperature record in key Pacific zone: EU monitor
item.description: Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino would likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode’s expected peak later this year Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
item.description: Australia's normally dry, rust-colored outback has erupted into a spectacular carpet of wildflowers after unusually heavy rains, potentially producing its most impressive bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellite images capture the stunning transformation, which has even brought rare flowers to the grounds of a remote deep-space observatory. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Rescued weather records reveal hot days became nearly twice as common in the Congo Basin over two decades
item.description: New research led by Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) and published in the journal Earth System Dynamics shows a clear warming signal across the Congo Basin since the 1960s, using historical weather records from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These records come from the paper archives of the Institut National pour l'Etude et la Recherche Agronomiques (INERA) in Yangambi, DRC, and the State Archives of Belgium. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
item.description: Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: University of Glasgow develops £20 ultrasound device to produce fertiliser from air and water
item.description: Researchers at the University of Glasgow have developed an affordable ultrasound device to produce nitrate for agriculture. This device uses sound waves, air, and water to create nitrate without industrial production reliance. While current experiments show potential, energy consumption remains high compared to the Haber-Bosch process. The team plans to refine the design over the next year for practical agricultural use. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Scientists discover vanilla’s hidden healing potential
item.description: Scientists have discovered that vanillin, the compound that gives vanilla its distinctive flavor, has powerful properties that could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and promote wound healing. The inexpensive, widely available ingredient could one day become an important component of advanced wound treatments and regenerative medicine. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep
item.description: Getting better sleep might be as simple as moving a little more every day. Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin found that people who exercised more frequently experienced more deep, restorative sleep, which is essential for brain recovery, memory, and emotional well-being. Surprisingly, just 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day was associated with measurable benefits, while even light activities like walking and standing breaks were linked to better sleep and mood. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Wildlife populations have declined 73% since 1970—but many of the world's animals still aren't being counted
item.description: Wildlife populations around the world have declined by an average of 73% since 1970. That's according to the WWF's new 2026 Living Planet Index—a major estimate, updated every two years, of the changing state of nature. This does not mean that 73% of the world's animals have disappeared. Rather, it is the average decline in the size of wildlife populations being monitored. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'DNA Typewriter' records cells' history in developing mouse embryo
item.description: Scientists have succeeded in reconstructing the family tree of cells in a developing mouse embryo. They recorded cells' relationships, starting when the fertilized egg first split in two and ending after the body and its organs took shape. That period lasted 13.5 days. (Full gestation in mice is 19 to 21 days.) Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments
item.description: Mathematics may hold unexpected clues to understanding Alzheimer’s disease. Scientists have developed a model showing how common metals like copper and zinc may influence the buildup of proteins associated with the disease, while also exploring possible ways to stop the process. The findings could help researchers identify promising strategies for preventing harmful plaque formation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Quantum 'birthmarks' hold lasting traces of a system's past
item.description: Some classical physical systems can explore many configurations over time until their long-term behavior no longer reveals their starting conditions. The sampling of available configurations according to the appropriate statistical distribution is a property called ergodicity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New study shows effects of hypoxia in Florida's Banana River
item.description: A new study by Florida Tech assistant professor of marine sciences Austin Fox, Ph.D. '15, found that low oxygen levels are contributing to the rerelease of nutrients buried on the river floor that feed harmful algal blooms. The study was based on the most widespread testing ever of oxygen levels across the Banana River. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Conservation groups alarmed at marine mammals' deaths in Spain
item.description: Conservation groups on Sunday condemned the death of a dolphin transferred from France to a Spanish marine park, saying it added to the deaths of other sea mammals recently moved to Spain from Canada. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Indonesia releases eight orangutans rescued from fires to protected forest
item.description: Eight orangutans rescued in recent weeks from blazes that tore through Borneo island have been released into a protected forest, Indonesian authorities and rescuers said on Sunday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the universe's fundamental physical constants may be finely balanced to make life possible. Even tiny changes to these constants could make liquids too thick or too thin for essential biological processes, potentially preventing life as we know it. Surprisingly, these life-friendly conditions existed billions of years before living cells appeared. The findings raise intriguing questions about why the laws of physics seem so well suited to life. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: La profesión más antigua del mundo tiene 40.000 años y está en un yacimiento de Barcelona
item.description: Si hay algo que nos ha ayudado a conocer mejor a los neandertales, esos son sus retos: huesos fosilizados, dientes y objetos como herramientas de piedra o cenizas. Al fin y al cabo, es lo que sobrevive al paso de 40.000 años porque el resto se pudre. Sin embargo y tras cuatro décadas de excavación en un yacimiento en Capellades (Barcelona), un equipo del Institut Català de Paleoecologia Humana i Evolució Social (IPHES-CERCA) ha encontrado 597 huellas de un material que no aparece en las quinielas de la supervivencia: madera. Aunque el concepto de "oficio" no aplicaba por aquel entonces porque… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk
item.description: An international team of researchers has uncovered new evidence illuminating the evolutionary origins of one of the defining features of mammals: the ability to suckle and consume milk during infancy. Their findings, published in Nature, suggest that key anatomical structures required for mammalian suckling, swallowing and breastfeeding behaviors evolved nearly 165 million years ago, long before the appearance of modern mammals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: A South Korean container ship returned on Sunday from a trial voyage through the Arctic, testing an alternative route opened by melting sea ice as conflict in the Middle East disrupts global shipping. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA spots a giant patch of Moon-like rock on Earth
item.description: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed a remarkable formation in Madagascar that looks surprisingly similar to the Moon’s bright highlands. Made of anorthosite, a rock abundant on the lunar surface, the formation dates back at least 600 million years and bears the scars of ancient continental collisions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Egypt's Fayoum mummy portraits to travel abroad for first time after restoration
item.description: Egypt unveiled Sunday a restored version of the "Tondo of the Two Brothers," a prized second-century painting from the famed Fayoum portraits. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New injection makes fat cells self-destruct
item.description: Scientists have developed an experimental injection that destroys fat cells and significantly reduces dangerous belly fat, potentially opening a new path to treating obesity. Early research also suggests it could help prevent the weight regain that often follows stopping popular weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: Researchers at the Mubadala Arabian Center for Climate and Environmental Sciences (ACCESS) at NYU Abu Dhabi have developed a new algorithm that can forecast Arctic sea ice extent up to nine months in advance, offering a new way to anticipate changes in the Arctic that can affect the global climate system. The research is published in the journal Scientific Reports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spinach nanoparticles help failing rat hearts via 'borrowed photosynthesis'
item.description: A spinach leaf can turn light into chemical energy. A struggling heart cannot. Researchers in China have brought part of the leaf's energy-making machinery into rat heart cells to test whether borrowed photosynthesis could help an overworked heart. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: NASA has launched a washing-machine-sized spacecraft to inspect up to four inactive satellites and rocket bodies in low Earth orbit. The SSPICY mission, launched on October 1, will begin inspections in early 2027. Using autonomous navigation, sensors and electric propulsion, the spacecraft will test technologies that could eventually help repair satellites or remove orbital debris. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Wild horses and donkeys dig desert wells in Arizona, supplying water to 57 vertebrate species
item.description: Researchers studied wild horses and donkeys in the Sonoran Desert, which dig wells that attract diverse wildlife. The wells serve as critical water sources for various vertebrate species during dry periods. Observations indicated that these wells significantly increase water accessibility and create favorable conditions for cottonwood seedlings. The study highlights the animals' role as ecosystem engineers in changing their environment. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: The eye has a hidden cleanup system scientists never knew existed
item.description: Scientists have discovered a hidden cleanup system at the back of the eye that drains fluid and waste through a previously unknown pathway. The surprising finding, demonstrated in mice, could open the door to new treatments for glaucoma, macular degeneration, and other causes of blindness. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Eating olive oil before carbs has a surprising effect on blood sugar
item.description: A simple change in the order you eat your food could help prevent blood sugar spikes. Scientists discovered that giving mice olive oil before carbohydrates slowed digestion and activated a surprising combination of hormones and nerve signals that helped regulate blood sugar, even in mice with type 2 diabetes. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists build a nuclear clock that could make atomic clocks obsolete
item.description: Scientists in Vienna have achieved a major breakthrough in timekeeping by creating the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a technology that could eventually surpass even the most precise atomic clocks. Instead of relying on electrons in atoms, the clock uses the tiny nuclei of thorium atoms, which are far less sensitive to outside disturbances. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A plastic once thought harmless may be fueling fatty liver disease
item.description: One of the world's most common plastics may pose a hidden threat to liver health. Texas A&M researchers discovered that polyethylene microplastics can contribute to fatty liver disease, with potentially worse effects when combined with an unhealthy diet. Even more surprising, this widely used plastic was previously considered relatively harmless. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Neanderthals may have used prehistoric glue as an ancient antibiotic
item.description: Neanderthals may have used a sticky substance made from birch bark to treat wounds thousands of years before antibiotics existed. Researchers recreated ancient birch tar production techniques and discovered that every sample could inhibit the growth of bacteria responsible for dangerous wound infections. Previously known mainly as a prehistoric glue, birch tar may have doubled as a surprisingly effective natural medicine. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Zimbabwe's dinosaurs were different from South Africa's: New species offers clues
item.description: Africa boasts up to 25% of Earth's animal and plant species. This diversity is driven by varied habitats: harsh deserts, vast grasslands, dense forests, towering mountains, lush coastlines and teeming seas. It is also due to deep evolutionary roots, as many animal and plant groups originated here in the distant past. Paleontologists have been excavating this material for nearly two centuries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists created a tiny device that can control your nerves to treat chronic pain
item.description: Scientists have developed a tiny, injectable device that can control nerve activity without surgery, batteries, or wires, potentially transforming treatment for chronic pain and movement disorders. Powered wirelessly from outside the body, the seed-sized technology has shown promising results in early testing. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A surprisingly simple way to relieve knee arthritis pain without pills or surgery
item.description: A surprisingly simple change in how you walk could help relieve knee arthritis pain and even slow joint damage. In a year-long clinical trial, researchers found that adjusting the angle of a person's foot while walking reduced osteoarthritis pain by an amount comparable to medication, without requiring drugs or surgery. Even more promising, MRI scans revealed that participants who adopted the personalized walking technique experienced slower deterioration in a marker of knee cartilage health. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: The brolga holds an important place in Gunditjmara culture and is an indicator of wetland health, but their numbers are under threat. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Ultraviolet laser pulses engineer diamond defects selectively, leaving quantum qubits intact
item.description: When we think about a diamond, we often think about a material whose value comes from its perfection. In my research, however, I am interested in something almost opposite: the tiny imperfections inside diamonds. These atomic-scale defects can give diamonds new optical and electronic properties, and some of them can serve as quantum systems. The challenge is learning how to control these defects without disturbing the others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trump lashes out at Zelenskyy over rising diesel prices in the US
item.description: US President Donald Trump blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for sky-rocketing fuel prices shortly after he said he had brokered a diesel supply deal with Russia. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.description: Meal prepping is a great way to save money, spend less time in the kitchen and stick to a meal plan. But while cooking meals for the week ahead may be convenient, there can be real risks associated with eating bulk-cooked meals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: As a teenager, Gillian Maegan Montalbo's pimples weren't too bad—just a few bumps on her forehead and nose. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists may have found a shortcut to fusion energy
item.description: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory may have found a dramatically more efficient route to fusion energy by reversing the traditional approach: heating plasma first, then increasing its density. Their calculations could help future reactors reach self-sustaining fusion with far less energy while avoiding hidden problems that make ignition harder. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Loneliness may steal nearly 6 years of good health
item.description: A large study suggests loneliness and social isolation can cost people years of healthy life, especially when it comes to mental health. Men experiencing both lost about 5.8 years free from depression and anxiety, while women lost roughly 3.7 years. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: MIT astronomers catch a star in a feast that could last billions of years
item.description: Astronomers have discovered a bizarre star system about 300 light-years from Earth where a small star is slowly devouring a nearby brown dwarf, an object too massive to be a planet but too small to be a true star. Unlike stars that rapidly swallow their companions, this one is gradually stealing material in a process that could continue for billions of years. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Bowel cancer “melted away” after immunotherapy, then stayed away
item.description: A short course of immunotherapy before surgery may offer remarkably durable protection for some patients with stage two or three bowel cancer. In the NEOPRISM-CRC trial, 32 patients with a specific genetic form of bowel cancer received pembrolizumab for up to nine weeks before surgery instead of the usual post-surgery chemotherapy. After nearly three years of follow-up, none of the patients had experienced a cancer recurrence, including those who still had small traces of disease after treatment. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
